title: Things to Do in Aswan in One Day: Philae, the High Dam and the Unfinished Obelisk
excerpt: Things to do in Aswan in one day: the Unfinished Obelisk, the High Dam and Philae Temple, plus a sunset felucca. Costs, the best order and shared tours from €36.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

The three things to do in Aswan that fit one day are the Unfinished Obelisk, the Aswan High Dam and Philae Temple on Agilkia Island. A guided circuit takes about five hours with hotel pickup, and costs from €36 per person with tickets, motorboat and lunch included, as listed in November 2026. The afternoon and sunset belong to a felucca, a traditional wooden sailboat.

UNESCO explains the Nubian monuments and the international rescue of Abu Simbel and Philae.

Key facts

Fact Detail
Where Aswan, southern Egypt, on the Nile: Egypt's southernmost major city and the gateway to Nubia
Main sites Unfinished Obelisk (northern granite quarries) · Aswan High Dam · Philae Temple, the Temple of Isis, on Agilkia Island
Time needed About 5 hours for the three sites on the Sawa shared tour; a full day with a felucca sail or a Nubian village visit
Typical cost Sawa shared day tour from €36 per person, as listed in November 2026, including entry tickets, motorboat and lunch. Philae entry alone is EGP 550 (about €9) per foreign adult if you travel independently
Opening hours Philae daily 07:00 to 16:00, with last entry reported at about 15:00. Unfinished Obelisk reported 07:00 to 17:00. The High Dam is a viewpoint stop; confirm hours locally
Best time to visit October to April, with early starts: Aswan is one of Egypt's hottest cities
Getting there A flight from Cairo takes roughly an hour and a half. The three sites sit 10 to 30 minutes apart by road; Philae is reached only by motorboat
Good for Solo travellers, couples and families: short walks, one boat ride and gentle steps at Philae
Join it on Sawa Aswan Highlights: Unfinished Obelisk, High Dam & Philae, from €36 per person

Aswan is usually the afterthought of an Egypt trip: a night at the start or end of a Nile cruise, or a stop before the very early drive to Abu Simbel. Yet the city's three headline sites fit into one unhurried morning, and the order you visit them in matters more here than almost anywhere in Egypt. This post gives a one-day route and the real costs. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours), the Egypt shared-departure marketplace, lists Aswan tours with live prices, and its founder has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

Things to do in Aswan in one day: the short answer

Visit the Unfinished Obelisk first, the Aswan High Dam second and Philae Temple last. That order follows the sun and the boats: the quarries are coolest early in the morning, the dam is a short viewpoint stop, and Philae, the longest stop, closes at 16:00 with last entry earlier (as of November 2026). A shared departure covers all three in about five hours, so the afternoon stays free for a felucca. A second day, if you have one, belongs to Abu Simbel.

The one-day Aswan route, stop by stop

This is the order of the Aswan Highlights shared tour, about five hours with a licensed guide (as listed in November 2026):

  1. Pickup at your Aswan hotel. Hotel pickup is included.
  2. The Unfinished Obelisk, still attached to the bedrock of the northern granite quarries, a short drive from the centre.
  3. The Aswan High Dam, a viewpoint stop: Lake Nasser to the south, the old 1902 dam to the north.
  4. Philae Temple, reached by a short motorboat ride across to Agilkia Island. It is the longest stop of the day, as it should be.
  5. Lunch on the way back into town.
  6. Back in Aswan, with the whole afternoon still ahead of you.

Doing it independently follows the same order. The three sites sit 10 to 30 minutes apart by taxi, no guide is required to enter, and you buy each ticket yourself: Philae costs EGP 550 per foreign adult and EGP 275 for students, plus the boat (as of November 2026). Reports say many Egyptian sites now take cards only, so carry a card. You trade a guide's stories for a pace of your own.

Philae Temple: the Temple of Isis on Agilkia Island

Philae is the jewel of the day: the Temple of Isis, rebuilt block by block on Agilkia Island after the High Dam's rising waters threatened the original island. The Aswan Low Dam of 1902 had already left Philae partly submerged for much of each year. The move, carried out between 1972 and 1980 as part of UNESCO's campaign to save the monuments of Nubia, re-erected the temple on higher ground nearby. Worship of Isis continued here into the 6th century AD, so Philae was among the last places in Egypt where the old religion was practised. Give it time: the first pylon of Ptolemy XII, the birth house of Horus and the waterfront kiosk of Trajan.

Philae opens daily at 07:00 and closes at 16:00, with last entry reported at about 15:00 (one 2026 visitor guide lists a 15:00 closing, so check on the day). Independent visitors who arrive soon after opening usually find a quieter island.

The Unfinished Obelisk: Aswan's 1,000-tonne mistake

The Unfinished Obelisk is the largest known ancient obelisk: a shaft of roughly 42 metres and an estimated 1,000 to 1,200 tonnes of granite. It is thought to have been commissioned by Queen Hatshepsut in the 18th Dynasty, more than 3,500 years ago, and was abandoned when a crack appeared while it was being freed from the bedrock. It still lies attached to the northern quarries, and that is what makes the stop: the trench around it shows how the ancient masons worked, and the dolerite pounding stones they used, harder than the granite itself, still lie in the pits. Aswan's granite went into obelisks that now stand in Luxor, Istanbul, Rome, London and New York.

The Aswan High Dam: why Philae had to move

The Aswan High Dam, begun in 1960 under President Nasser and completed in 1970, is modern Egypt's great engineering landmark: it ended the Nile's annual flood, stores the river's flow in Lake Nasser and generates hydroelectric power. Its cost was Nubia's landscape: the rising lake threatened Philae and submerged the land behind it, triggering UNESCO's rescue campaign. For visitors it is a viewpoint, not a walking site: Lake Nasser stretching south, the lotus-shaped friendship monument, and the smaller British-built dam of 1902 downstream.

If you have longer: feluccas, Nubian villages and Abu Simbel

One day covers Aswan's essentials; three extras reward a slower stay:

  • A sunset felucca sail. An hour around Elephantine Island and past Kitchener's Island, the Aswan Botanical Garden, is the classic close to an Aswan day.
  • A Nubian village visit. Communities such as Gharb Soheil on the west bank welcome visitors with painted houses, hibiscus tea and Nubian hospitality.
  • Abu Simbel. The temples of Ramses II and Nefertari stand about 280 km to the south; the Aswan to Abu Simbel shared tour picks up at your Aswan hotel very early and drives 3.5 to 4 hours each way through the Nubian desert, with routine checkpoints (carry your passport). The day takes about 9 hours, with tickets and lunch included, from €50 per person, as listed in November 2026. Twice a year the sun reaches the inner sanctuary: see our guide to the Abu Simbel sun festival.

Because the Abu Simbel day ends in the afternoon and Philae stays open until 16:00, an independent visit to Philae afterwards is possible, though it makes for a very long day. Sawa does not sell the two as a combined tour. Travelling north afterwards? The Kom Ombo, Edfu and Esna temple road turns the drive to Luxor into a temple day, from €60 per person, as listed in November 2026.

The verdict on one day in Aswan

One well-ordered morning, the Unfinished Obelisk, the High Dam, then Philae by motorboat, sees Aswan properly, with the afternoon left for a felucca and the evening for the corniche. faq.q: Is one day really enough for Aswan?
faq.a: For the headline sites, yes. The Unfinished Obelisk, the Aswan High Dam and Philae Temple fit into about five hours, leaving the afternoon free for a felucca sail. What one day cannot fit is Abu Simbel, which needs a separate 9-hour day. If you want both, stay two nights.

faq.q: Can I visit the three sites without a tour?
faq.a: Yes. The sites sit 10 to 30 minutes apart by taxi, no guide is required to enter, and you buy each ticket yourself: Philae costs EGP 550 per foreign adult, plus the boat, as of November 2026. A shared tour from €36 with tickets, boat and lunch included often costs little more than going alone, with a licensed guide as well.

faq.q: What is the best time of day to visit Philae Temple?
faq.a: Morning. Philae opens at 07:00 and closes at 16:00, with last entry reported at about 15:00 (as of November 2026). Arriving near opening means a quieter island.

faq.q: Can I see Abu Simbel and Philae on the same day?
faq.a: It is possible but very long. The Aswan to Abu Simbel shared tour takes about 9 hours from a very early hotel pickup, and Philae stays open until 16:00, so an independent afternoon visit can fit. Sawa does not offer the two as one tour; most travellers give Abu Simbel its own day and keep Aswan slow.

faq.q: Is Aswan safe for solo travellers?
faq.a: Aswan is regularly described by visitors as one of Egypt's calmer cities, and its sights are compact and easy to reach. On a Sawa shared departure you move around with a group of up to eight and a local licensed guide, and our WhatsApp line, +20 109 284 7613, is answered 24/7 while your tour is running. The usual city precautions apply, as anywhere.

faq.q: What happens if the Aswan date I reserve doesn't fill?
faq.a: Nothing is charged before a date reaches four travellers and gets the GoAhead. A date has until 7 days before the tour to reach four; if it does not, it is cancelled, you pay nothing, and we suggest another date. Once a date is confirmed, it is not cancelled for low numbers: if someone does not pay after the GoAhead they are excluded and the tour still runs for everyone else.
